input.question: I understand from the news that if we don't bomb Syria our reputation will take a major hit internationally. Why do we care about our reputation internationally?
input.ground_truth: Our President warned publicly that the use of chemical weapons (weapons of mass destruction) against civilians would constitute a dangerous line to cross in escalating the conflict. Syria used them anyway, in a blatant manner which couldn't avoid notice. Therefore the President has to make it clear that such warnings are not in vain; there will be some sort of consequence from violating such a warning, otherwise future warnings can be ignored as toothless (re: North Korea).

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: I understand from the news that if we don't bomb Syria our reputation will take a major hit internationally. Why do we care about our reputation internationally?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let's imagine you have lots of friends at school. When you play nicely and follow the rules, your friends think you are a good friend to have. They want to play with you again and trust you.

Countries are a bit like that. When a country like ours does what other countries think is right, or at least tries to be fair, other countries want to be friends with us and trust us. If we do something really mean or break the rules (like bombing another country without a good reason), our friends (other countries) might not want to play with us anymore. They might not trust us or listen to us when we want to talk.

So, when people talk about our "reputation" internationally, they mean how other countries see us. If our reputation is good, other countries are more likely to like us, work with us, and trust us. If our reputation is bad, it can be harder for us to get help or make friends in the world. That's why we care about our reputation internationally.
